response:
Continual fine-tuning asks a foundation model to sequentially absorb new task distributions without losing competence on old ones — but gradient descent has no built-in memory, so each new update overwrites weight configurations that encoded prior knowledge. The central question here is whether the order and mixing ratio of data batches during fine-tuning causally determines how fast that forgetting accumulates, and whether deliberate curriculum design (as opposed to random shuffling or naive sequential exposure) can slow the decay curve. The key concepts in tension are: (1) gradient interference — new-task gradients pointing in directions that damage old-task loss landscapes; (2) replay and mixture ratios — how much old-domain data must be co-present in each training batch to act as a forgetting brake; and (3) curriculum ordering — whether easy-to-hard, domain-similarity-sorted, or interleaved schedules meaningfully change the geometry of the loss surface traversal.

What a beginner misses is that catastrophic forgetting isn't a single failure mode — it has at least two distinct signatures that respond differently to curriculum interventions: representational drift (the model's internal feature space rotates away from old-task geometry) and decision boundary collapse (task-specific head weights get overwritten while representations stay intact). An expert worries that a curriculum fix solving one signature can actively worsen the other, and that evaluations measured only at end-of-training mask the trajectory of forgetting, making a bad curriculum look identical to a good one if the final checkpoint happens to land in a similarly mediocre spot.

Convergence at the final checkpoint absolutely does not vindicate checkpoint-only evaluation — it conceals at least two deployment risks that are invisible to that metric. First, if a model passed through a deep forgetting trough mid-training, the weight trajectory may have crossed into a basin with worse generalization geometry even if loss values recover: Frankle et al.'s lottery ticket work and subsequent sharpness-aware minimization literature (Foret et al., 2021) suggest that which basin you land in matters for out-of-distribution robustness, and two runs can match in-distribution accuracy while sitting in basins of dramatically different flatness. Second, in production, models are rarely static — they get further fine-tuned, quantized, or adapted via LoRA patches, and a model whose weights passed through a forgetting trough may be significantly more brittle to these subsequent interventions; this is essentially the plasticity-stability debt problem, where the trajectory burned plasticity that the final checkpoint loss doesn't reflect. Concretely, Luo et al.'s 2023 work on fine-tuning order in instruction-tuned LLMs found that models with identical MMLU scores post-training showed divergent degradation rates under subsequent domain adaptation — the checkpoint metric was blind to this fragility. A third risk is calibration: a model can recover task accuracy through weight configurations that are overconfident or miscalibrated on old-task inputs, which ECE (expected calibration error) would catch but top-1 accuracy at checkpoint would not. The practical implication is that curriculum evaluation needs at minimum three probes beyond final accuracy: loss basin sharpness (e.g., SAM-style perturbation), post-hoc fine-tune stress tests, and calibration curves — all of which require looking past the checkpoint into what the training trajectory built.

The sensitivity is unfortunately high and asymmetric: set the threshold too low and you trigger replay so frequently it collapses into standard fixed-ratio mixing (losing the curvature-targeting benefit entirely); set it too high and you miss sharpening events until the optimizer has already committed to a bad basin, at which point replay can recover accuracy but not basin geometry. Empirically, in SAM-adjacent literature, basin flatness measured by the sharpness metric ρ (the perturbation radius at which loss increases by ε) can degrade by 3-5× with threshold miscalibration even when final accuracy is within 1% — which is exactly the hidden-risk problem from the previous turn reappearing at the hyperparameter level. The most principled threshold-free alternative is to replace the fixed scalar with a relative curvature ratio: compare current Fisher trace to a running exponential moving average of Fisher trace over the past K steps, and trigger replay when the ratio exceeds some multiplier (e.g., 1.5× the EMA) rather than an absolute value — this self-calibrates to the model's own curvature history and doesn't require knowing the absolute scale of Fisher values, which varies enormously across architectures and learning rates. A second principled approach borrows from control theory: treat the Fisher trace as a signal and the replay rate as a control variable, then use a PI controller (proportional-integral) to adjust replay intensity continuously rather than via binary threshold crossing — this eliminates the threshold entirely and has precedent in adaptive learning rate schedules like AdaGrad. The deeper problem both approaches share is that Fisher trace is a global summary statistic, so it can be low on average while individual layer curvatures are dangerously high — Zhao et al.'s 2023 work on layer-wise forgetting heterogeneity shows that forgetting in transformers concentrates in attention layers 40-60% of depth, meaning a global threshold will systematically miss localized sharpening events that drive the worst forgetting.

Selective layer replay is mechanistically appealing and partially validated: if attention layers at 40-60% depth are the primary forgetting locus, freezing or upweighting replay gradients there while letting later layers adapt freely should in principle protect the representational geometry where old-task information lives. Biderman & Raiman's 2023 work on selective layer freezing during fine-tuning, and separately Lee et al.'s work on surgically fine-tuning only specific transformer components, both show that restricting gradient flow to forgetting-prone layers can preserve old-task performance with 30-40% less replay data — a significant efficiency gain. But here is what breaks: transformers are not modular in the way this intervention assumes. Residual stream representations are cumulative sums across layers, so freezing gradient updates at layer K while allowing updates at layer K+1 creates a gradient mismatch where later layers adapt to a representational basis the earlier frozen layers no longer consistently produce — this manifests as subtle distribution shift in the residual stream that doesn't show up in layer-wise metrics but degrades end-to-end task performance in ways that are hard to diagnose. A second failure mode is that selective replay gradients change the effective learning rate schedule implicitly: layers receiving replay gradients see a different gradient variance than layers that don't, which can destabilize LayerNorm statistics and produce training instability that looks like a data problem but is actually an optimization geometry problem. The principled fix — used in parameter-efficient methods like LoRA applied selectively to attention projections — is to not freeze layers but instead scale replay gradient magnitude by layer-wise Fisher importance, allowing all layers to update but with old-task gradient influence proportional to each layer's measured forgetting contribution, which avoids the residual stream mismatch while still concentrating protective signal where it matters most.

LoRA does structurally reduce catastrophic forgetting, but for a reason that's more subtle than "low-rank updates touch fewer weights": by confining updates to a rank-r subspace of each weight matrix, LoRA implicitly restricts gradient flow to directions that span the new-task signal, and if old-task representations live predominantly in the orthogonal complement of that subspace, they are largely preserved by construction. Biderman et al.'s 2024 "LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less" paper quantifies this directly, showing that LoRA fine-tuning on code and math domains forgets significantly less of the base model's language capabilities than full fine-tuning at matched training compute — but crucially, forgetting is reduced, not eliminated, because the low-rank subspace is not perfectly orthogonal to old-task directions, especially at higher ranks (r=16 or r=64) where the adapter begins approximating full fine-tuning. Curriculum ordering remains highly relevant for two reasons. First, the subspace LoRA learns is itself order-dependent: if early training batches establish the rank-r basis in a direction that interferes with old-task geometry, later batches cannot easily correct this because the adapter's principal directions are approximately set by the dominant gradient signal seen first — a curriculum effect operating entirely within the low-rank constraint. Second, when multiple LoRA adapters are composed (as in multi-task or sequential adapter stacking), the interference between adapter subspaces is strongly influenced by the order in which they were trained, with earlier-trained adapters occupying subspace directions that later adapters must work around. The practical implication is that LoRA changes the scale of the curriculum ordering problem but not its existence: at rank r=4, ordering effects are modest; at r=64, they approach full fine-tuning severity, meaning curriculum design remains essential for any deployment using higher-rank adapters or adapter composition.

Yes, and this idea has been partially realized in GradOrth and OrthogonalFinetuning (OFT) style methods: the initialization strategy would compute the top-k eigenvectors of the old-task Fisher (or a Kronecker-factored approximation thereof), then initialize LoRA's A and B matrices such that their product AB spans the null space of those eigenvectors — placing the adapter's update directions where old-task curvature is lowest from the start. Wang et al.'s 2023 OFT paper shows that constraining fine-tuning updates to preserve the hyperspherical energy of weight matrices (a proxy for Fisher-orthogonal updating) reduces forgetting substantially while matching LoRA's parameter efficiency, and Zeng et al.'s 2024 DARE/TIES merging work implies that orthogonal initialization gives adapter merging significantly better interference properties than random initialization. The erosion problem is the hard part: standard gradient descent has no mechanism to enforce subspace constraints during training, so even a perfectly orthogonal initialization drifts as the optimizer follows new-task gradients that have components in old-task Fisher directions — the orthogonality half-life depends on learning rate and new-task gradient magnitude, but in practice significant drift occurs within the first 5-10% of training steps. Three mechanisms can slow erosion: (1) a projection step after each gradient update that re-orthogonalizes AB against the Fisher eigenvectors — computationally expensive but exact; (2) an auxiliary penalty term added to the loss that penalizes the Frobenius norm of the projection of AB onto the Fisher subspace — cheaper but introduces a new hyperparameter; (3) reducing the learning rate specifically for adapter directions that show increasing Fisher-subspace overlap, essentially a directional learning rate schedule. The fundamental tension is that perfect orthogonality maintenance is equivalent to projecting away any new-task gradient component that overlaps old-task directions, which is only safe if new-task and old-task signals are truly separable in weight space — if they share important directions (as they often do in shared linguistic structure), enforcing orthogonality doesn't prevent forgetting so much as prevent learning, trading one failure mode for another.
